name: Zero, first and second conditional
subtitle: Use if + present simple for facts and real, possible situations: If it rains, we'll stay in. Use if + past simple + would for imaginary or unlikely situations: If I had more time, I would learn Spanish.
source: icanspeak English original English text (grammar-b1 run, 2026-10-29)

concept.exampleHtml: If it rains, we'll stay in. — If I had more time, I would learn Spanish.

qa.html: Zero conditional: if + present simple, present simple. Use it for facts and things that are always true. If you heat ice, it melts. If I don't sleep, I get a headache. Here if means almost the same as when.

First conditional: if + present simple, will + verb. Use it for a possible situation in the future and its result. If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay at home. If you study, you'll pass the exam. The if part uses the present simple, even though it is about the future.

Second conditional: if + past simple, would + verb. Use it for imaginary or unlikely situations now or in the future. If I won the lottery, I would travel the world. If we had a garden, we would get a dog. The past simple here does not talk about the past. It shows that the situation is not real.
Put the if part first and use a comma: If it rains, we'll stay in. Put it second and use no comma: We'll stay in if it rains. The meaning is the same.

Typical mistakes: ✗ If it will rain tomorrow, we'll stay in. → ✓ If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay in. (no will after if) · ✗ If I would have more money, I would buy a car. → ✓ If I had more money, I would buy a car. (no would after if) · ✗ If I will see her, I tell her. → ✓ If I see her, I'll tell her.

concept.noteHtml: In the main clause you can also use can, could, might or should: If you hurry, you might catch the train. If I had a car, I could drive you. For advice, people often say If I were you, I'd … After I, he, she, it, were is the careful form. In everyday speech many people say If I was you, and that is fine too. For if and when in future sentences, see When or if. For will and other future forms, see Future forms. For would and could as modal verbs, see Modal verbs.

items: If I were you, I'd take the earlier train.
If I were rich, I'd travel the world.
Careful English: were after I, he, she, it.
Everyday speech: If I was you, … is also common.

boxes.badge: No will or would after if
items: ✗ If it will rain, … → ✓ If it rains, …
✗ If I would win, … → ✓ If I won, …
The result part has will or would. The if part does not.

rounds.label: 1 · Real: if + present, will
rounds.instruction: You hear two short ideas. Join them in a first conditional: If + present simple, will + verb.

example.prompt: it's sunny – we go to the beach
example.answer: If it's sunny, we'll go to the beach.

items.prompt: Tom is late – we start without him
items.answer: If Tom is late, we'll start without him.

items.prompt: I see Amira – I tell her
items.answer: If I see Amira, I'll tell her.
If it snows, the trains will stop.

items.prompt: you study hard – you pass the exam
items.answer: If you study hard, you'll pass the exam.

items.prompt: we miss the bus – we walk
items.answer: If we miss the bus, we'll walk.

rounds.label: 2 · Imaginary: if + past, would
rounds.instruction: You hear two ideas. Join them in a second conditional: If + past simple, would + verb.

example.prompt: I win the lottery – I buy a house
example.answer: If I won the lottery, I would buy a house.

items.prompt: I have more money – I travel more
items.answer: If I had more money, I would travel more.

items.prompt: Kwame lives near the sea – he swims every day
items.answer: If Kwame lived near the sea, he would swim every day.

items.prompt: we have a garden – we get a dog
items.answer: If we had a garden, we would get a dog.

items.prompt: I speak French – I work in Paris
items.answer: If I spoke French, I would work in Paris.

items.prompt: she has more time – she learns the piano
items.answer: If she had more time, she would learn the piano.

items.prompt: they have a car – they drive to work
items.answer: If they had a car, they would drive to work.

exercises.title: Choose the right form.
exercises.hint: Is it a fact, a real possibility or an imaginary situation? The if part uses the present simple or the past simple, never will or would.
exercises.hintHtml: factif + present simple, present simple.real possibilityif + present simple, will + verb.imaginaryif + past simple, would + verb.

items.prompt: If you mix blue and yellow, you ___ green.
items.why: This is always true (a fact). Use the present simple: get.

items.prompt: If it rains tomorrow, we ___ at home.
items.why: Tomorrow is a real possibility. After if + present simple, use will + verb.

items.prompt: If I ___ a million pounds, I would buy a boat.
items.why: Would buy shows this is imaginary. The if part uses the past simple: had.

items.prompt: Amira would be happy if you ___ her.
items.why: Would be happy is a second conditional. The if part uses the past simple: called.

items.prompt: If you ___ the bus, you'll be late.
items.why: You'll be late is a first conditional. The if part uses the present simple: miss.

items.prompt: What ___ you do if you saw a mouse in your kitchen?
items.why: Saw is the past simple, so the main part needs would.

items.prompt: If I ___ you, I'd phone the doctor.
items.why: If I were you is the usual advice phrase. Was is also common in speech.

exercises.title: Which conditional is it?
exercises.hint: Zero: a fact. First: a real possibility, with will. Second: imaginary, with would.
